# I identified the device that was being used to take over the account and blacklisted it and removed it from the victim user. Meaning that going forward that device will likely get 3DS challenges and it won’t impact the victim user
# Interesting finding: the victim made another [order|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/delivery-order/orders/183431539?cityId=386] after the incident and the gps location of the user during creating that order and the [fraud order|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/delivery-order/orders/182849129?cityId=386] are in the same spot. Can’t rule it out that it is a coincidence, but it is curious. I wouldn’t dare to say that this is evidence that both orders were done by the same person, most likely it is a coincidence, but still good to be aware of.
# Also another person can’t just login into another user’s account. There can be two options:
## either the victim shared the SMS auth code with the fraudster which enabled the fraudster to log into the victims account (meaning that the victim is liable for the incident)
## or the victims phone number was recycled and the “fraudster“ took advantage of gaining access to an account which still had usable cards
# Timeline of the order and card removal:
## Order was created on 13.07.24 at 19.53 (local time)
## The price of the order (27.25€) was authorized and booked on 13.07.24 at 19.53 (local time)
## The card was removed  on 13.07.24 at 20.03 (local time)
## The payment was captured on 13.07.24 at 20.11 (local time)
## When the funds get booked then it is already too late and it doesn’t matter whether the card was removed or not. The capture will still take place
# The victims account is what we in the Fraud team consider a “spender with good history” and hence we apply rules to reduce imposed friction (3DS challenges for example) and therefore the “fraud order” was not 3DS authorised
# Overall I would say that the biggest question is how the “fraudster” was able to log into the victims account (see point nr. 3). I believe that that will determine on whom the liability will fall to.

I'm sorry for not getting back to you sooner.

Transparent reporting is not only a primary request from our largest business customers in Georgia but also a vital component for maintaining loyal relationships with them. Additionally, there is a legal requirement to ensure that all pricing components are visible to the service recipients.

Specifically, the [Law of Georgia on the Protection of Consumer Rights|https://matsne.gov.ge/en/document/view/5420598?publication=0] mandates in Article 5, under the basic obligation to provide information to a consumer, that:

"d) the price of the goods or services, specifying basic and additional charges (including charges necessary for transportation, re-sending, and installation of the goods, etc.), and where the nature of the goods or services does not allow the calculation of the price in advance, a rule for calculating such price, and the information that additional charges may be payable."

This law also includes Chapter VII, which covers Institutional Guarantees for the Protection of Consumer Rights if this article is not considered.

Furthermore, according to the Final Price Breakdown (UTC) Looker Dashboard, 20% to 23% of the total GMV of all RH rides in Georgia comes from the wait time fee component.

Considering the legal, statistical, and user feedback mentioned above, it is crucial to show the waiting time in the monthly CSV. 

Regarding your last question, I believe it makes more sense to show the total amount of paid waiting time in the monthly CSV rather than the cost.



Regards,
Otto

Additional restriction at the airport should be fine, for now.

* search_id = unique query across all providers

* pickup_lat, pickup_lng = pickup coordinates
* destination_lat, destination_lng = destination coordinates
* service_provider = provider name
* service_level = ride type (standard, XL, etc)
* product_name = service name
* price_min, price_max = usually the same unless a range is provided for the estimated price
* surge_multiplier = multiplier above regular price level
* eta_seconds = estimated time to pick up the passenger
* duration_seconds = estimated time from pickup to destination

 AUTO_ID_CACHE=1 has no effect on write hotspots.

The problem arises when there’s large table, but all the reads and writes are localised within very ‘narrow’ part of it - if reads/writes are concentrated within one or very few single regions (chunks) of data located at the same storage node. 

Batch import is not something that matches this pattern, but rather something like 1M rows table where only last 100 are constantly updated and read.

After multiple hours of debugging the conclusion is the following:

The bug comes from the {{listAllObjects}} method in {{S3ModelStore.java}}. The issue is that the code copies every object having a certain _prefix_ i.e. not every object within a “folder”. In practice, if the input prefix path is {{models/delivery-h3-cold-distance-matrix/v2.1/<date>/cities/4}}, {{listAllObjects}} will return every object in {{models/delivery-h3-cold-distance-matrix/v2.1/<date>/cities/4}}, as well as every object in {{models/delivery-h3-cold-distance-matrix/v2.1/<date>/cities/40}}, {{models/delivery-h3-cold-distance-matrix/v2.1/<date>/cities/401}} etc.

In our case, the bug reproduced in the following conditions:

* we’re performing a partial recompute
* city 401 has some new providers to compute estimations for
* city 4 does not have any new computations to perform
* the worker thread for city 401 uploads the provider.bin and header.bin files at T0
* the worker thread for city 4 copies the old files at T1
* the worker thread for city 401 uploads the data.bin file at T2

So we are left in an inconsistent state where the provider and header files contain old info, while the data file contains new info.

The following job runs fail because the new provider are found in the data files, but cannot be extracted from the providers.bin file (we have an explicit check in the code for this).

The other thing to note here is that having incompatible header and data files causes the returned estimations to be mixed up: the index for a particular cell is not where we think it is, so we actually return estimations for a different cell. This is very likely what caused the issue reported here [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/GDEXP-277|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/GDEXP-277|smart-link]  and the incident in Kosice reported here [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C011C71M220/p1721299729872789|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C011C71M220/p1721299729872789|smart-link] 

A final note on reproducibility: this issue has likely silently existed for a long long period of time. In fact, in the 3-4 runs that happened before the crash _all_ files were overwritten by a different city thread. This didn’t crash the job though, because the model was perfectly valid - it was essentially a copy of the previous model. This time around we got lucky and got in an inconsistent state that made the job crash and allowed us to properly investigate.

The main question here is: *Who is controlling the tool? Bolt, or the CS Provider?*

*If Bolt*, then from the initial overlook of the data protection clauses, *I’d push for concluding an additional DPA*, preferably our template. Let’s see what the business' answer will be.

On a general note the current data protection clauses are missing some explicit obligations and prohibitions that are important for us, including but not limited to:

* The scope and purpose of personal data processing: to the extent necessary to provide the services and in accordance with our instructions and notifying us if this was breached + prohibition of sale of the data
* Confidentiality: while the technical and safety obligations are there, the processor must ensure that all employees, agents, officers and contractors involved in the handling of the supplied personal data are aware of the confidential nature and are bound to keep this data confidential
* Sub-processor information: we’d like a list of sub-processors as well as be able to have a prior authorization of any new sub-processor + the sub-processors obligations towards us and that the processor is fully liable for the acts/omissions of sub-processors + prohibition of restricted transfers of personal data
* Audit: we’d like our processors to have an obligation to provide information to demonstrate compliance and to reduce Bolt's audit rights and that the costs are borne by them
* Data breach notification: in case of breach, we’d like to be notified within 24 hours
* DSARs: we’d like to be notified within 24 hours and at processors' expense
* DPIAs: at processors' expense when we need assistance
* Liability of the processor for breaches of the DPA and full indemnification for losses incurred from processor’s failures (technological and human), I think I only saw liability & indemnification clause only for data breaches
* Deletion of data after the end of the agreement: we’d like processors to continue to ensure the compliance with the DPA until the data is deleted / returned (if processor has to keep some data for longer)

Hi [~accountid:712020:5c3f18cd-53ab-40ca-9fae-fb38035ab6d8], 

Similar to how this is dealt with in Norway (which we have discussed before), when a person in Sweden or a company declares bankruptcy, their assets are typically transferred to a bankruptcy estate. The bankruptcy estate is managed by a trustee appointed by the court. The primary purpose of the bankruptcy estate is to liquidate the assets of the bankrupt entity and distribute the proceeds to creditors according to the established priority of claims.

The estate has certain rights against creditors that the creditors are obliged to respect. The purpose of the bankruptcy estate is that the estate shall “step into the shoes” of the bankruptcy debtor and seize all the debtor’s assets and claims.

The Court order states that the lawyer in the document is appointed as the “trustee” and represents the bankruptcy company so no additional PoA is required. The law firm has the right to receive information about any outstanding funds and transactions between the company and Bolt. 

This is the standard position in Sweden so please keep this in mind for any future requests. In short, ss long as we have the court order stating who the trustee is we can release the information to them. 

Thank you!

In this case, the agents could reach out to confirm the mask of the card, however the user has already been advised to contact their bank - the outcome would remain the same regardless. Hi [~accountid:5f718abb25fbdf00681557a5] , getting back to you with my insights.

* First of all, there is a fine line between a generic request to receive company data and a GDPR request.
* For example, generally, only the driver himself will be able to request a copy of his data or to request his data to be erased under GDPR. 
* Therefore, as per our process, we ask the Fleet to provide proof of authorization from the driver to the fleet in case the fleet is submitting a GDPR request on behalf of the driver.
* Having said that, I believe that most of the points you posted can be sensitive from GDPR perspective, so I’d like to get more clarification:
**  I want to change my banking details: A user requests for their bank details to be changed
*** Who is *_user_* in this case?
*** Whose bank details are requested to be changed?
**** If payouts are made directly to the fleet and the fleet needs to change their bank account details - there should be no issues from privacy side.
**** If payouts are made to the drivers and the fleet wants to change the details of the driver’s bank account - we need to follow the process in Beehive KB for driver bank data change.
** I want to change my driver details: A user wants to change their driver's account details
*** Who is *_user_* in this case?
*** What account details we mean, can you specify?
*** Generally, this could be treated as a GDPR request if we are speaking about changing the driver’s details, so it should go through Beehive KB process for Driver data change.
** I want to request a document: A user wants to get a document from Bolt e.g. Earnings report or a Tax report, etc. 
*** Who is *_user_* in this case?
*** Generally, this could be treated as a GDPR request if we are speaking about receiving the driver’s data, so it should go through Beehive KB process for Driver data request.
** I want to request my personal data: Fleet Owner requests personal data Bolt holds of them
*** Not a privacy concern - should be consulted with Legal/other teams, as this is not personal data. We just need to make sure that personal data of the fleet drivers is not included in the response.
** My account has unrecognised activity: User suspects that someone has used their credentials to access their account or they have received information meant for someone else
*** This might indicate that a data breach has happened - the privacy team needs to be informed immediatelly and a SD ticket to privacy needs to be submitted.
** I want to delete my account: A user requests for their account to be deleted
*** Who is *_user_* in this case?
*** Generally, this could be treated as a GDPR request if we are speaking about deleting the driver’s data upon fleet’s request, so it should go through Beehive KB process for Driver data deletion request.
** I want to request personal data of the driver: Fleet Owner wants to get access to driver's personal data
*** Generally, this could be treated as a GDPR request if we are speaking about receiving the driver’s data, so it should go through Beehive KB process for Driver data request.
*** We should ask for proof of authorization if the fleet wants to receive the driver’s personal data
** I want to change my fleet registration address: A user requests for their registration address to be changed
*** no comment - all good from privacy
** I want to delete my driver’s personal data: Fleet Owner wants for driver personal data to be deleted
*** Generally, this could be treated as a GDPR request if we are speaking about deleting the driver’s data upon fleet’s request, so it should go through Beehive KB process for Driver data deletion request.
*** Proof of authorization needs to be received
** I want to report driver's fraud: A user wants to report their fleet driver does some fraudulent activity
*** no comments from privacy
** I want to request order history: A user requests the order history that Bolt holds of them
*** is there any personal data? If so, this could be treated as a GDPR request if we are speaking about receiving the driver’s data, so it should go through Beehive KB process for Driver data request.
** I want to delete my personal data: Fleet Owner wants to delete all personal data that Bolt keeps about them
*** Should go through GDPR data deletion process, same as there
** I want to object to the use of my personal data: Fleet Owner objects how Bolt uses its personal data, including automated-decision making conducted by Bolt 
*** Should go through GDPR Beehive process, same as there
** I want to delete my order history: Fleet Owner requests for their history to be deleted
*** Do fleet owners have order history?

Hi [~accountid:5a6703100645002e2794a3f0] , adding some examples, as discussed. As we spoke, the idea shouldn’t be to scare people with millions of fines, but we can add some examples from below on what happens when data is not protected properly - and that the regulators do care about it.



* *Marriott International (2018)*: Marriott announced a data breach that affected up to 500 million guests of its Starwood hotels. The breach involved personal information such as passport numbers, email addresses, and phone numbers. The UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) initially issued a £99 million fine, which was later reduced to £18.4 million​ ([Enzuzo|https://www.enzuzo.com/blog/biggest-gdpr-fines])​​ ([SecurityWeek|https://www.securityweek.com/medical-company-fined-450000-by-new-york-ag-over-data-breach/])​.
* *Ticketmaster (2018)*: Ticketmaster was fined £1.25 million by the ICO for failing to protect customer data. The breach, which occurred between February and June 2018, affected 9.4 million Ticketmaster customers across Europe. The incident involved a third-party chatbot installed on the payments page of the Ticketmaster website, which allowed attackers to harvest personal and payment information​ ([Enzuzo|https://www.enzuzo.com/blog/biggest-gdpr-fines])​​ ([SecurityWeek|https://www.securityweek.com/medical-company-fined-450000-by-new-york-ag-over-data-breach/])​.
* *British Airways (2018)*: In September 2018, British Airways experienced a data breach affecting approximately 500,000 customers. The breach involved personal and financial details, including credit card information. The UK Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) initially proposed a fine of £183 million, but it was later reduced to £20 million due to the financial impact of the COVID-19 pandemic​ ([Enzuzo|https://www.enzuzo.com/blog/biggest-gdpr-fines])​​ ([SecurityWeek|https://www.securityweek.com/medical-company-fined-450000-by-new-york-ag-over-data-breach/])​.

# checked which field is better to use ({{user_phone_anonymized}} or {{user_phone_prefix}})
# which table to use to refer to country phone code (dim_city is generally enough, but might not be enough for country-level measurement markets)
# Checked with raw query that:
##  user_phone_prefixes are collected correctly for a city
## a city normally does not have a lot of weird phone numbers (only the 0del-s)



!raw_vs_complete_query.png|width=663,height=713,alt="raw_vs_complete_query.png"!



The query:

**

{noformat}%sql 
         SELECT --'Signups Locals Only' AS metric_name 
               DATE(u.user_created_date) as date_date
               , COALESCE(city.city_name, 'other') AS city
               , COALESCE(city.country_name, 'other') AS country
               , CASE WHEN u.user_app_version LIKE '%CA%' THEN 'android'
                    WHEN u.user_app_version LIKE '%CI%' THEN 'ios'
                    ELSE 'other'
                END AS os
              ,sum(case when user_phone_prefix = city.country_phone_prefix then 1 else 0 end) as signups_locals
              ,sum(case when user_phone_prefix != city.country_phone_prefix then 1 else 0 end) as signups_nonlocals
           FROM core_models_spark.dim_user u 
           LEFT OUTER JOIN core_models_spark.dim_city city
             ON u.user_home_city_id = city.city_id
          WHERE u.user_created_date >= date('2023-01-01')
        GROUP BY 1,2,3,4{noformat}

I understand that localizing the Bolt Send T&Cs has taken longer than expected, and I would like to explain why:

The global Bolt Send T&Cs for drivers provided by product counsel are designed exclusively for self-employed drivers and are intended to be applied alongside the Ride-hailing T&Cs. These global T&Cs specifically cover aspects of the package delivery service, referring to the Ride-hailing T&Cs for all other matters not explicitly addressed by the Bolt Send T&Cs. This means that drivers providing delivery services under the Bolt Send category must be bound by both sets of T&Cs.

However, this approach is not valid in Cyprus because the delivery services under the Bolt Send category will be provided by fleets and self-employed drivers who are limited to transporting only goods  and are not authorized to carry passengers according to local legislation.

Therefore, I had to create bespoke/standalone Bolt Send T&Cs for Cyprus, which:

# Cover both independent drivers and fleets, collectively referred to as transportation service providers.
# Include specifics of the package delivery service and general aspects of the Ride-hailing T&Cs (liability, fees, in-app payments, etc.), excluding provisions related to passenger transport. This ensures that the Bolt Send T&Cs in Cyprus do not apply alongside or in addition to the Ride-hailing T&Cs, as fleets and drivers under the Bolt Send category in Cyprus are not allowed to transport passengers and should not be bound by T&Cs that reference passenger transport.

After completing the localization myself, external counsel conducted a review and translated the T&Cs into Greek. External counsel has also confirmed that Bolt, as an intermediary platform, is not required to apply for any postal service license or notify any authority about this activity.

I am also take this opportunity to share templates for communications to announce the launch of Bolt Send, in case they are of interest to you: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_dUR9BLfy9o4jc7kOOzbwnaPbEwP4Us2GOpnSt-Ygoc/edit#heading=h.4lym375p3c86|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_dUR9BLfy9o4jc7kOOzbwnaPbEwP4Us2GOpnSt-Ygoc/edit#heading=h.4lym375p3c86|smart-link] 

Lastly, I recommend including the following disclaimer/warning for the Bolt Send category in both apps (Clients and Transportation Service Providers):”_This category is designated exclusively for the transport of packages. According to legal regulations, it is strictly prohibited to use transportation services provided under this category for the transportation of passengers. We kindly remind users to adhere to these guidelines for the safety and compliance of all parties involved.”_

I’ve been asked to provide a Greek translation of the above disclaimer, which will follow shortly.

Many thanks!

If we start from far, then fleet system already differs in EE from other markets. 

Since fleet owners are pretty busy, they are not always able to request the removal of the driver from the fleet after the driver has returned the vehicle. 

In addition, fleet does not know in which direction driver will proceed (and driver is not obliged to give his answer right away): will he become a private driver or will he exchange to another fleet. Until this is unclear, driver remains under the last fleet (group) he was. 

There may be days and weeks passing after driver has made his decision.

We can not limit driver when he wants to exit the fleet, and we have to act quick. It is *not the best approach* to make driver run here and there in order for his vehicle to be accepted.

Hi [~accountid:712020:0641ea87-e832-482b-8673-ab85e9ad6441] 

Regarding what we spoke about on the issue of legal framework for this service, please find some remarks below:

* It looks like the best legal framework for this service is the provision of postal services, regulated by Law 17/2012, available here: [https://www.pgdlisboa.pt/leis/lei_mostra_articulado.php?nid=1953&tabela=leis&so_miolo=|https://www.pgdlisboa.pt/leis/lei_mostra_articulado.php?nid=1953&tabela=leis&so_miolo=]
* According to this law the following services can be considered postal services:  the delivery of a postal parcel, which is a package containing goods or objects with or without commercial value (article 5). 
* In the old drafting of the Law there was a height limit for it to be considered a postal service corresponding to the delivery of a postal parcel. It looks like this not the case anymore, according to the new drafting. 
* Regarding licenses: the law establishes a universal regime (which works like a minimum limit which is ensured by CTT) and generic regime (for all other companies providing postal services). 
* Bolt would be included in the generic regime, meaning it only needs a general authorization, and no license, according to article 24/1-b) of the law. 
* The regulator in this case is ANACOM, so they general authorization should be given by them. It should be requested through the online portal, according to article 25. 
* The general authorization request should contain the elements referred to in article 34 and following. 
* By going through this route we would be excluded from the applicability of law on the transportation of goods, as per article 2/4, available here: [https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/detalhe/decreto-lei/57-2021-167133018|https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/detalhe/decreto-lei/57-2021-167133018]



Therefore, next steps: 

* Make an explicit reference to the postal service law in the T&Cs, stating that this is considered a postal service. 
* Request a general authorization to ANACOM to start operating as a provider of postal services.

Hey there!
Just as a reminder here of wha’ts needed here : 

# WD does not reflect properly the time off balances for _FRA Annual Leave_ (= CP) :
#* We need to *differentiate CP N & CP N-1* as it is on Bolt France employee payslips. CP N relate to the current year accrual of _FRA Annual Leave_ on a monthly basis (so +2,08 CP each month). Per company agreement, the accrual period is from 01/01/N till 31/12/N so on 31/12/N everyone should normally be at 25 CP N and on 31/01/N+1, those 25 CP N are transferred into 25 CP N-1 balances and the CP N balance is credited of 2,08.
Those CP N-1 are to be used before 31/12/N+1, otherwise they expire as of 01/01/N+2.
#* End of year CP N *balance are rounded up* when tranfered to CP N-1 balance (for example 1,4 CP N on 31/12/N become 2 CP N-1 on the 01/01/N+1.
#* Per voluntary application of the SYNTEC CBA, *every threshold of 5 years of seniority* (till 20 years) *grant +1 CP per year*. Therefore, if you have 5 years of seniority, during year N, on year N+1 (i.e. on 01/01/N+1 in practice) you get +1 CP N on top on the 25 usual ones accrued per year.

*Legal background*

The matter is regulated by Regulation (EU) 2018/848 on organic production and labelling of organic products (particularly Art. 34 thereof) and Agriculture Ministry Order no. 45/2022 implementing the registration procedure. As per Art. 34 para. 2 of Regulation (EU) 2018/848, operators that sell pre-packed organic products directly to the final consumer or user shall be exempted from the notification obligation referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article and from the obligation to be in the possession of a certificate referred to in Article 35(2) provided that they do not produce, prepare, store other than in connection with the point of sale, or import such products from a third country, or subcontract such activities to another operator. 

Bolt selling bio products that are produced, packed and labelled by someone else as part of Bolt Market is exempt from the registration procedure and requirement to hold a certificate provided Bolt complies with the requirements.

*Requirements that will apply to Bolt*

Bolt must only declare its activity to the local agriculture office and fulfil the following obligations:

a) to request from the supplier and hold at the point of sale certificates for all products distributed (certificates issued in accordance with Art. 35 para. (1) of Regulation (EU) 2018/848); - _in our case we should keep certificates both electronically and at the dark stores_.

b) to notify the  local agriculture office in the event of changes in the activities they carry out that require registration in organic farming;

c) to separate products obtained from organic production from those obtained from conventional production. 

+_The exception does not apply where Bolt is the one distributing the product (including where it first affixes the Romanian language label) or where it operates a central warehouse for multiple retail units._+

*Next steps*

We need to make sure that we can get relevant certificates and inform the local agriculture office about our activity. My non-legal take on this.

In Ireland, anyone can make a claim against a service provider, employer, city, etc.… if they have been injured and feel it was no fault of their own.

The Injuries Resolution Board is a pre-court, cost effective means of doing such. Most people will opt for this route as it avoids going through a costly litigation process.

Our options are this;

# We consent to the claim being assessed by the board - this means they will determine what payout the injured party is to get. A fee of 1,050 EUR is required to process the claim. We should notify insurance if going down this route. This means we are accepting responsibility.
# We ignore the claim and ultimately consent by default - this means we do not reply and a fee of 1,050 EUR is required to process the claim. We should notify insurance if going down this route.
# We respond by stating we do not consent to the claim - in this event the the board will release the case and its up to the claimant to go down the costly litigation route if they wish.

Hi [~accountid:712020:ab95f96b-73f1-4bb8-a5fd-5178ef3f1339] and [~accountid:712020:46da73ea-bcbb-4b69-8e3e-ac27402d61bc] I would like to raise a few points in relation to this complaint that we should discuss internally before sending out a final response. 

+*A - PRICE FARES AND TOLLS*+

+*Price of TVDE service in accordance with TVDE Law*+ 

* According to TVDE law, the provision of the TVDE service may be remunerated by (a) applying one or more tariffs to the distance travelled and/or the time spent in transport, *or* (b) by applying a fixed price determined before the service is contracted. My understanding is that Bolt is under option (b): Bolt on behalf of the TVDE operator makes available a predetermined fixed price proposal, which, if accepted by the passenger, corresponds to the price to be charged at the end of the service regardless of the distance travelled or the time spent. 
* The same law establishes that there is a *principle of freedom* regarding the setting of tariffs and price, with the following *limitations*:
** the intermediation fee may not exceed 25 % of the value of the trip;
** the dynamic tariff may not exceed the value resulting from the application of a 100 per cent mark-up factor to the average value of the price charged for the services provided in the 72 hours immediately preceding that operator;
** *final prices must cover all costs associated with the service*, in line with best practice in the transport sector.
* Bolt has the following *information obligations* in relation to the *passenger*:
** provide information in a clear, understandable and objective manner, *before the start of each ride and during the ride*;
** inform the *price calculation formula*, indicating in particular the *total price*, the i*ntermediation fee* applied *and the applicable fares*, namely by distance, time and dynamic fare factor;
** an estimate of the price, calculated on the basis of the information provided by the user and the weighting factors that make up the formula for calculating the price to be charged by the service operator.

+*Toll price*+ 

The toll price is not listed in the fare price in the Bolt app as correctly indicated by the driver. We do indicate that “the price estimation can change if actual tolls/surcharges differ from estimation (city based)” However, how can a user know the price calculation formula is not correct if no information on the toll/surcharges in indicated in the app? This means that *we are arguably missing the information on one element of the price formula before and during the ride: the toll price. Failure to comply with the TVDE law may lead to a fine (5k to 15k) and interdiction of the licence to operate up to 2 years.*

Even though this obligation does not seem to cover drivers, but only passengers, it would appear reasonable that the drivers have visibility on the amount of tolls/surcharges since the price of each service must cover all the associated costs. How can drivers verify the price of the tolls/surcharges for each service? My understanding is that there is screen on the app where this information is currently available.

* {color:#006644}*_Recommendation: add information on toll amount in the Bolt app before and during the ride._*{color}

+*Price and service costs*+

Final prices must cover all costs associated with the service following the TVDE law. *How have we implemented the requirement that the price covers all the service costs, particularly:*

*  *on rides where minimum fare is applied (which includes all additional costs and intermediation fee)?* In the case shared the ride is for 1,5km and the driver is arguing that the net price of the ride was 2,89 euros (where 1 euro was the parking fee).
* *on rides much longer than estimated due to traffic?* In the case raised by the driver the estimated ride was for 47 minutes and it ended up being 93 minutes. Was there a price review for this case?
* *on rides with tolls?* I understand that there are operational constraints to maintain the toll prices accurate in the app. Such limitations may reduce the amount of potential fines, but IMO does not takes away Bolt’s responsibility to ensure compliance with this legal requirement.

*Failure to comply with the TVDE law may lead to a fine (5k to 15k) and interdiction of the licence to operate up to 2 years.*

+*B - DEFINITION OF TERRITORIAL SCOPE TO RECEIVE RIDE REQUESTS*+

It appears we have a feature in the driver app where the driver can set a radius (such as 1KM) to receive ride requests. The radius defined for accepting rides is a straight line distance and the driver can be assigned a ride to make within it, but for which the driver may have to travel a longer distance to the passenger. In the occasions where a driver within their defined radius is not found, the system shares the rides to drivers outside their default radius. This is beneficial to the passenger that is seeking a ride and driver that will receive further ride requests. 

*Could you please confirm whether the rejection in this case has impact in the driver score or acceptance rates which are visible in the driver app?* Is there information on the website on this matter or that we have made available to the drivers and tvde operators?

Thank you.

Hi [~accountid:62cbe709c4c3be001fb4a674], here are my thoughts on this matter:

* The [Subsidiary Legislation 499.68 the “Light Passenger Services and Vehicle Hire Services Regulations”|https://legislation.mt/eli/sl/499.68/eng/pdf] that regulates RH services in Malta determines that {{19.An operator shall not have the right to refuse to provide light passenger transport services to any hirer except on reasonable grounds, including, when it is clear from his demeanour, that the hirer is under the influence of drugs or alcohol or where the safety and security of the driver may be at risk.}} The law does not specify whether this situation would be considered reasonable, but having wet clothes or sand is very different from the examples provided in the law (alcohol , safety). Therefore, I see a risk that advising drivers that they have the right to decline passengers if they are likely to wet the car seats could be seen against the local legislation.
* I also would advise against recommending drivers to provide seat covers to protect their vehicles as this could be seen as Bolt determining how the transportation services are to be carried out, which is one of reclassification criteria in the Employment Status National Standard Order (S.L 452.108): {{3.(1) Subject to the provisions of sub-article (2), whenconsidering the employment status of a person who is nominallyself-employed and is prima facie not considered as an employee, itshall be presumed that there is an employment relationship and thatthe person for whom the service is provided is the employer andthat the provisions of the Act and of the regulations or orders issuedthereunder apply to that relationship if at least five of the following}}: …{{(b) he depends on the person for whom the service is provided to determine what work is to be done and where and how the assigned work is to be carried out}}
* Our t&c foresee such situations very clearly in clause 4.14:  _If, in the course of the provision of the Transportation Services, a Passenger or its co-passengers negligently damage the vehicle or its furnishing (among else, by blemishing or staining the vehicle or causing the vehicle to stink), you shall have the right to request the Passenger to pay a penalty up to 50 EUR and request compensation for any damages exceeding the penalty. If the Passenger does not consent to paying the penalty and/or compensating the damage, you must notify us and we will then try to collect the penalty and/or relevant costs on your behalf from the Passenger. However, bear in mind that we are not taking any liability for direct or indirect damages in relation to cleaning or maintenance of the vehicle caused by Passenger._ 
* To avoid potential abuse of the right above I would recommend you to consider establishing a more detailed list of cleaning fees depending on the mess and Bolt Offers with cleaning companies. In Portugal last year the local operations worked on this matter given similar concerns related with abuse. I suggest that you contact [~accountid:5f0c30effe23000022252e68] who might give you more insight on this matter.

Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Hi All, I confirmed with our Czech legal counsel that we do not have to issue a physical receipt in this case and electronic one will be fine. Please ensure that the receipt contains all the elements according to the below cited provisions_._ I am also copying the full opinion that we received just for us to have it here.



_From the point of view of consumer protection law, you are particularly concerned with the following obligations (I am sending a literal translation of the legal provisions):_

 +_At the consumer's request_+_,_ +_the seller is obliged to issue a receipt for the purchase of the product or the provision of the service_+_, indicating the date of sale of the product or the provision of the service, what the product or service is and at what price the product was sold or the service was provided, together with the seller's identification data containing the name and surname or the name or business name or business name of the seller, his personal identification number, unless a specific legal regulation provides otherwise._

# _In the case of the sale of products with subsequent delivery, the document shall also contain the destination and the date of delivery._
# _In the case of the sale of used or modified products, defective products or products whose performance is otherwise restricted, these facts must be clearly indicated on the document._

 _It follows that the regime you mention in your email will apply. Please ensure that the receipt contains all the elements according to the cited provisions. Regarding receipts in the tax area, your accountants will help you to prepare the documents properly so that they meet the legal requirements._

 _With regard to the possibility of issuing the document electronically,_ +_I confirm that the electronic issue of the requested document is possible_+_. Such a regime applies in particular to contractual relations with a consumer where the contractual obligation is concluded electronically, without the physical presence of both parties. I have consulted Czech Trade Inspection, which has confirmed that such a procedure is legal. If there was an element of the consumer's physical presence in the contracting process, then the need to issue the required document in paper form could be considered - I assume this does not apply to you as all contracting is done electronically via your application. If you really want to be fair, you can ask your customers to agree to electronic delivery of these documents as part of the new customer registration process. Then there will be no doubt that your customers will agree to this procedure from the beginning._

 _Please note that the above-mentioned legal regime does not apply to the so-called "confirmation of transport", which you send to customers on behalf of the carrier on the basis of the Road Transport Act. This document must be sent after each transport, even without a request from the customer (it can be sent electronically), with the formalities according to the law._

Whoever makes preparations for the offence specified in § 1, shall be subject to a fine, the penalty of restriction of liberty or the penalty of deprivation of liberty for up to 2 years.

# KSB does not specify the categorization of video surveillance under the national data protection laws, however, they listed all specificities for video surveillance requirements in order for it to be legal - words it as subject to data protection laws if the records capture persons and they can be identified, or data on the registration plates
# *Requirements for collection:*

* At least on one of the Article 6(1) GDPR grounds (+recommending 6(1)(f) GDPR legitimate interest+ but can also be used in combination with other legal bases)
* In compliance with Article 5 GDPR

# *Registration of collection activity:* not provided in the memo
# *Possibility to submit request for Data Protection Inspectorate to issue opinion:* Not provided in the memo
# *DPIA:* Necessary
# *LIA:* Necessary (if we’ll rely on legitimate interest) - in case of dispute/complaint, Bolt must prove that balancing exercise was done to consider if legitimate interest of the controller outweighs individual’s right to privacy
# *Informing the DS:* Necessary to inform the DS in a banner at a visible place - information about the ongoing surveillance, name of the controller, contact details, purpose of the processing, and link to website where more detailed information can be obtained (visible warning sign, preferably in addition to English also in Czech). There must also be an indication of the possibility to obtain other information specified in Article 13 GDPR & keep records pursuant to Article 30 GDPR.
# *Retention & Retention Period:* Necessary to adhere to minimization of video cameras, recordings of surrounding areas, implementing privacy-friendly technologies, and minimization of persons having access to the recordings, deletion without delay after the expiration of the retention period - to the extent necessary to achieve the purposes (even though not specified in the memo, assuming EDBP Guidelines 2/2019 apply). KSB recommends to keep the retention periods limited to the extent necessary to achieve their purpose. If records are shared publicly, personal data must be anonymized. KSB warns about audio recordings and vehicle tracking functions - legality will be more questionable. Audio recording of the cabin may be permissible where it can contribute to clarifying the course of the damage event of traffic accident. KSB recommends minimizing the interference with DS rights when it comes to localization and route tracking. 
# *Obligations towards processors:* Necessary to ensure the compliance requirements of the processors and proper DPA, SCCs if needed and have a proper documentation.
# *Other comments:* Bolt is required to process and keep complete documentation of the on-board cameras.
# *Conclusion:* The Data Protection Inspectorate decisions / guidelines are consistent case-law of the CJEU and EDBP guidelines

Hello,

As discussed via Slack, the reclassification risk for couriers in Cyprus is currently assessed as moderate (Level 2).

To provide a clearer picture of the Cypriot market, it's essential to differentiate between two types of couriers and their associated risks:

* *Independent Couriers*: These individuals work as self-employed contractors. The primary risk for this group is the potential for their reclassification as Bolt employees.
* *Fleet Couriers*: These couriers are employed by fleets. The risk here involves potential issues related to employee lending, as the relationship between fleets and couriers might be seen as an assignment of employees to Bolt by the fleet.

Should the performance of couriers influence their order allocation or result in their removal from certain tags, this could potentially increase both reclassification and employee lending risks.

Although addressing courier performance may increase these risks, it is important to note that the current risk level in Cyprus is still moderate. Therefore, the decision to accept these potential increased risks ultimately rests with the business.

If you need any further information or clarification, please do not hesitate to reach out.

Many thanks.

{code:sql}with enrollments as (
select 
	e.*,
	t.name as treatment_group,
	tt.name
from ng_public.targeting_enrollment e
join ng_public.targeting_treatment t on e.treatment_id=t.id

where t.test_id in (10431)     
)
select treatment_group, platform, sum(rides), sum(gmv) from (
select 
o.user_id, 
e.treatment_group,
substr(o.user_app_version,1,2) platform,
count(distinct o.id) rides,
sum(o.charged_price) gmv
from enrollments e 
join ng_carsharing.rental_car_order_order o on o.user_id = e.auth_id 
where o.state = 'finished'
and o.created_date >= date'2024-07-01' 
group by 1,2,3
order by 5 desc 
)
group by 1,2
order by 2 asc, 1 asc {code}

Summary after the call with [@jevgeni.komkin|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U0735NPUR5H] (Head of Web) last week.

1] *First layer wording update.* [~accountid:712020:f0f7cc2d-5968-45e9-91ec-ea445d725066] `s suggestion is to update the banner with a bit more info on the purposes and incorporate Google`s ask to mention personalised ads purpose in the first layer. I believe it is reasonable and also beneficial for our compliance because:

* though we are not explicitly breaking the GDPR, and make available all relevant information under the GDPR / ePD, I see a risk of having a breach of the transparency principle by having the initial notice too basic.

* Our first layer of the banner is the briefest among competitors and other companies - this was analysed by the web team. IMO it would be beneficial for transparency if we included more info on the purposes in the initial view & added a link to the Cookie Declaration, which are available only in the second layer.

Currently, my suggestion to the web team is to add a little bit more info: in the following way:

Current version (first layer):

{quote}This website uses cookies.
We use cookies to ensure the best experience while browsing our website.{quote}

*Future version (first layer) - mentioning all purposes/categories of our cookies:*

{quote}_We use cookies for website functionality, to understand how you interact with the website, improve your browsing experience, and for ad personalisation._
_See [Cookie Declaration link] for more information._{quote}

The exact wording is still being discussed. As clarified by [@jevgeni.komkin|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U0735NPUR5H], the change would be easy to implement and they will take care of the translations (they want to rely on ChatGPT and content team manual review).

2] *Other changes.* Apart from the above, the only other change would be improving the UI to make it more explicit that we include the links to Google policies, which was another one of Google`s ask. As for the rest of their policy requirements, we can confirm to comply, as per my previous review.

3] *Response to Google*. Currently, the privacy team is aligning on the response to Google. Preliminary, the outline is:

{quote}_Dear Google Compliance Team,We have reviewed the policy requirements and would like to share our current approach while discussing how we can enhance transparency._

_Currently, we use a layered approach to deliver privacy information. Website visitors are informed that the site uses cookies and can choose to accept or reject them. For more detailed information on cookie usage, purposes and categories of cookies, third-party involvement (including mentioning Google and linking to Google’s privacy notices), and other privacy details, visitors can access preferences via the gear button and a link to the Cookie Declaration._

_We believe this approach aligns with GDPR and ePrivacy Directive regulations. However, we understand that our transparency could be improved. To address this, we have decided to add more information about the purposes of cookies on the initial screen. Following your request, we will also include the purpose of ad personalisation on this screen. Additionally, we will enhance the user interface to make the links to Google’s policy more evident and clickable._

_We hope these changes will address your concerns and improve user understanding while maintaining our compliance with privacy regulations.Thank you for your consideration. We look forward to your feedback. Please let us know if there are any other specific concerns that we can address._
_Best regards,_{quote}

Hi [~accountid:619df37d657a0500708b279a] 

*Summary:* the privacy team is able to confirm that Art. 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive (ePD) will apply to the tracking in question and will formally require consent for some purposes of the use of cookies.

Tracking can only be done based on one of two conditions where the ePD Art. 5 (3) applies:

* users provide their consents;
* tracking is necessary to provide Bolt services requested by the user. Note that it must be essential for the user to receive the service – helpful or convenient but not essential trackers will still require consent. 

As a general rule - it does not matter if the data is anonymised or not for the ePD Art. 5(3) to apply.

So, to answer your question:

* if the Mixpanel events are for analytics purposes that are necessary to provide the services and ensure that the services are provided correctly (ie load balancing, etc) - its ok not to rely on consent and categorise the cookies as necessary
* if the Mixpanel events are for analytics purposes which is not essential (ie to simply count how many users use a certain feature) - it requires consent.

Part B

# Notwithstanding subparagraphs B(1) and (2), the Reporting Platform Operator shall not be required to collect information referred to in points (b) to (e) of subparagraph B(1) and points (b) to (f) of subparagraph B(2) where it relies on direct confirmation of the identity and residence of the Seller *through an identification service* made available by a Member State or the Union to ascertain the identity and tax residence of the Seller.

Part C

# Notwithstanding subparagraph C(1), for the completion of the due diligence procedures pursuant to subparagraph F(2), the Reporting Platform Operator may determine whether the information collected pursuant to paragraph A, subparagraph B(1), points (a) to (e) of subparagraph B(2) and paragraph E is reliable, *using information and documents available to the Reporting Platform Operator in its electronically searchable records*.

Firstly, apologies for the wait. I have taken a look through this request and also the prior request by the Croatian police. It seems that the legal basis cited was valid. 

The two PDFs of the Croatian legislation that were linked in [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/405376815|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/405376815] are outdated, and the codes have been amended since then. 

Article 230 of the Criminal Code now reads: _‘Article 230: ‘Whoever, by using force against a person or by threatening to directly attack his life or body, seizes another's movable property with the aim of unlawfully appropriating it, shall be punished by imprisonment from one to ten years’._ This is a description of the relevant crime. 

Article 207 of the Criminal Procedure Act now reads: 'Article 207:

* (1) If there are grounds for suspicion that a criminal offense has been committed for which criminal proceedings are being initiated ex officio, the police have the right and duty to take the necessary measures:

# ﻿﻿﻿to find the perpetrator of the criminal act, so that the perpetrator or participant does not hide or escape,
# ﻿﻿﻿*to discover and secure traces of the criminal act and objects that can be used in establishing the facts* and
# ﻿﻿﻿*to gather all the information that could be useful for the successful conduct of criminal proceedings.*

In addition to granting the Police the right to collect data, this reads almost identically to the legal basis listed on the google doc for Croatia, so we are satisfied that it is a valid basis on which to share the data. 

With this in mind, the original data request can be satisfied, provided that the requested data is proportionate. Let the Police know that after further review of their request, we have decided to grant the data. 

If you have any further questions, just let me know through here. 

Thanks!

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

Hi [~accountid:627b6b92f29dcb0068f8d1e0] we currently dont have a policy/guidelines in terms of overall refund window. We are working on it tho, but might take some time. 

In regard to the main purpose of this request: _“the reason why I asked this in the first place is because we had localized our services in Italy (switched to an Italian Bolt entity), and Customer Support team is still receiving requests from pre-localization period where Bolt business details were different. Such refunds are causing us to issue invoices with the details of the pre-localization Bolt entity - which is not tax-compliant. Therefore, our plan is to stop refunding orders before localization. Hence the question of whether we are allowed to do this or not”_  

As said, we currently do not have an “overall refunds window” policy. This “refund window” is one of the things that should be included in this policy/guideline, and it depends on a lot of things. Regulations give you minimum in some cases. Some jurisdictions have regulations more favourable to consumers, and then comes the internal policy on refunds which should set a window for a refund request, among other things. For example, [Uber T&CS|https://www.uber.com/legal/en/document/?name=general-terms-of-use&country=republic-of-ireland&lang=en-gb] say any refund request window is 30 days after the order (they also say you do not have the right to claim a refund but if you do it can only be within 30 days after a completed order. After that is up to them to decide if they consider your request or not). 

*_“our plan is to stop refunding orders before localization. Hence the question of whether we are allowed to do this or not”_* 

*“Refunding orders before localisation”* is quite broad. What are the reasons for this requests? Today we do refunds based on a business decision/case by case scenario considering there is no overall window for refunds. However, it seems to be clear what are the cases when we should provide one. 

Having said that we currently do not have an “overall refunds window”, going ahead with these refunds request is a case by case, business decision. From which entity you complete the refund, is a question for accounting, tax or finance. 

From top of my head I say the refund should come from the same entity that receive the payment being refunded. However considering we are a group of companies, refunding from a different entity (in this case from the local subsidiary), should not be a big problem. It also depends on the numbers, how many refund requests from pe-localisation are we getting and for what? then we can determine what is the risk of being non complaint or what is the risk of refunding from a different group entity than the one which received the payment for the order.  

The answer to if you are allowed to do this or not is that depends on what the reason of the refund request is. As we do not have a window for refunds in our T&Cs (or not much at all about refunds actually), we cannot really say we deny your refund request because the time lapsed.

*What data we need to share with APAD*

* {{Ethnicity Data/Nationality}} is not deemed to be "_Sensitive Personal Data_", although in very specific cases involving users of the Malay race (who are Muslims), their Ethnicity/Nationality would infer Religion and would therefore be deemed Sensitive Personal Data.
* According to the local counsel, in additional to Ethnicity Data/Nationality, we also need to share a copy of the {{Driver's identity card }}as well as declarations by the Driver regarding their{{ state of health and criminal background }}—  [@afzan.lutfi|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U0746A3GEES] were you aware of this? [@alexandra.stoica|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U035W375BLK] FYI.

*Can we legally share this with APAD?*

* As I originally advised, {{the data protection law does not grant a specific exemption to share Sensitive Personal Data when required by a law or regulation}}.
* However, the local counsel is of the opinion that Bolt will nevertheless "*_likely_*" be able to share Sensitive Personal Data with APAD (due to the obligations set out in the APAD Circular and E-Hailing Guidelines). They justified this citing that Bank's are also currently legally required to share Sensitive Personal Data of their users to comply with a law (and are doing so), and that while Bolt is not in the Banking sector, the same exemption should apply.

*What does this mean for Bolt?*

* We can proceed with sharing the requested data with APAD, {{although there remains some risk involved in doing so.}} Based on the local counsel's feedback, we would classify the risk as low-medium and will not block such sharing at this point in time.
* [@afzan.lutfi|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U0746A3GEES], I would recommend that we enter into a Data Sharing Agreement with APAD. If they entertain this, I will try include some legal wording to protect Bolt when it shares this data with APAD. As a note, we have entered into numerous DSAs with other state authorities in the markets we operate.
* Before we share any data with APAD, we will need to obtain consent from Drivers during the registration stage. The consent will need to describe what data will be shared with APAD.

# *Registered address - consent should be given by WeWork before signing the contract*
“_If, subject to our prior consent, you are using an address provided by us as your registered address (…)_” As we want the premises to be our registered address, we need to be sure that WeWork will provide us with such consent.

# *Access to our office and alterations/relocations (clause 2 (b) of T&C)*
WeWork is entitled to access our office, move our furnishing or alter or relocate office space provided that it will not substantially decreases the square footage of our office space or related amenities. WeWork may also reasonably modify the scope of Services upon prior notice, provided that it will not reduce the number of your keycards or your credits.

+*Solution*+: Termination of the agreement or suspension of the services by WeWork should occur only after WeWork sends us a written request to cure the breach within e.g. 7 days and we do not cure this breach within given period.
# *Do we wish to implement a private wired network (clause 6 (viii) of the T&C)?*

Confluence guidance:

The supplier agreements should fit the following criteria:

# Liability-  no exclusion of liability clause should be included (e.g. seller is only liable in case of gross negligence). 
# Transport of the order- the supplier should carry out the transport of the order and there should be a fixed time for the delivery to be completed.
# Quality of goods- the quality has to be either "as agreed between the parties or, if no agreement has been made, generally acknowledged quality standards for similar kinds of goods".
# Certificates- the agreement has to set out that the goods hold all required certificates and comply with all applicable regulations in the applicable jurisdiction (e.g. regarding packaging, information on the package, instructions of use, CE-certificate etc) and the required documentation has to be delivered with the goods. 
# If the goods require specific temperature or similar conditions, then the agreement should set out that all requirements are met during delivery.
# Payment/ ordering- unless intended, there should be no monthly minimum order requirements or something similar.
# Notifying of deficiencies- i.e. the time period during which Bolt has to notify the seller regarding any deficiencies with the foods. This should be reasonable (e.g. not by the next day- in such case we might not have enough time to actually inspect the goods and make sure everything is in order).  
# Submitting additional orders- should be done in written format. 
# Local law should apply to the agreement.

The “types” are the following:

* UI (User Interface) events are sent from the app (or web), and are triggered as direct consequences of user’s behaviour – i.e. when they open a restaurant in Eater App.
* Server Side events are sent from Bolt servers (not app or web), and are not directly triggered by user, but instead they are indirect consequences of their previous behaviour – i.e. when courier marks Eater’s order as “Delivered” (it’s indirect consequence of Eater’s previous behaviour, as they’ve previously chosen to place an order in Bolt Food).

With our current implementation:

* UI events take into account user’s consent – if user hasn’t accepted cookies, we don’t send the MixPanel events.
* Server Side events do not take into account user’s consent – we always send the events, irregardless if the user has accepted the cookies or not.

She wrote: 

_I acknowledge the concerns raised in your email, and under the L.E.D. (Law Enforcement Directive), which is a separate instrument from the GDPR but still very much part of the 2018 Data Protection Act but particularly refers to Section 5 and “competent authorities”, of which are we, as a Department are. The relevant extract can be found below:_

_The Law Enforcement Directive, or ‘LED’, is a piece of EU legislation, parallel to the GDPR, which also has effect from May 2018. As suggested by its name, the LED deals with the processing of personal data by data controllers for ‘law enforcement purposes’ – which falls outside of the scope of the GDPR. The LED is a Directive rather than a Regulation, and this requires transposition into Irish domestic law to take effect. This transposition is achieved through the Data Protection Act 2018 (‘the Act’), primarily through ‘Part 5 – Processing of Personal Data for Law Enforcement Purposes’._

_The Data Protection Commission (DPC) is set out in Part 5 of the Act as the ‘independent supervisory authority’ for the LED._

_To Which Bodies Does the LED Apply?_

_It will be important to correctly identify cases in which the legal regime of the LED and Part 5 of the Data Protection Act 2018 applies. The LED regime only applies in cases where the data controller is a ‘competent authority’, and the processing is done for ‘law enforcement purposes’._

_However, this is not limited to processing by bodies who might be typically considered as ‘law enforcement authorities’ (such as An Garda Síochána), but to any processing for law enforcement purposes, carried out by a public or private body who fits the definition of ‘competent authority’ (such as local authorities when prosecuting litter fines, or Dublin Bus in relation to ticket offences). This means that a potentially very large number and variety of bodies might fall under the scope, and the applicability of this regime will need to be assessed on a case-by-case basis._

_There is effectively a two-step test to satisfy before you can determine whether the processing is question is within the scope of the LED and Part 5 of the Act:_

_firstly, the data controller responsible for the processing in questions must be a ‘competent authority’ as defined by Section 69 of the Act; but_

_secondly, the processing in question must actually be for ‘law enforcement purposes’, as defined in Section 70 of the Act._

_Bolt, as an agency, surely operates within the Taxi Regulator’s rules and regulations and therefore under the guidelines as published by the Department of Transport and TFI initiatives._

_I also note that you have stated to only engage in data sharing with third parties where you are satisfied that the requirements of your third party data sharing policy have been met, i.e., that requests be lawful, necessary, proportionate, and limited to the specific purpose outlined in the request. As our request for information is being carried out for the purposes of investigating and prosecuting criminal offences under law; per Section 70 of the Act, the L.E.D. and Part 5 may apply where the processing carried out by or on behalf of the controller is for any such purpose (highlighted in yellow). From the Act:_

_Application of Part 5_

_(1) This Part applies, subject to subsection (2), to the processing of personal data by or on behalf of a controller where the processing is carried out—_

_(a) for the purposes of—_

_(i) the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences, including the safeguarding against, and the prevention of, threats to public security, or_

_(ii) the execution of criminal penalties,_

_And_

_(b) by means that—_

_(i) are wholly or partly automated, or_

_(ii) where the personal data form part of, or are intended to form part of, a relevant filing system, are not automated._

_I further note that Section 71 (5) of the 2018 Data Protection Act also facilitates the release of data provided that requests are lawful, necessary, proportionate, and limited to the specific purpose outlined in the request (highlighted in yellow). See here:_

_Processing of personal data_

_(1) A controller shall, as respects personal data for which it is responsible, comply with the following provisions:_

_(a) the data shall be processed lawfully and fairly;_

_(b) the data shall be collected for one or more specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and shall not be processed in a manner that is incompatible with such purposes;_

_(c) the data shall be adequate, relevant and not excessive in relation to the purposes for which they are processed;_

_(d) the data shall be accurate, and, where necessary, kept up to date, and every reasonable step shall be taken to ensure that data that are inaccurate, having regard to the purposes for which they are processed, are erased or rectified without delay;_

_(e) the data shall be kept in a form that permits the identification of a data subject for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the data are processed;_

_(f) the data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the data, including, by the implementation of appropriate technical or organisational measures, protection against—_

_(i) unauthorised or unlawful processing, and_

_(ii) accidental loss, destruction or damage._

_(2) The processing of personal data shall be lawful where, and to the extent that—_

_(b) the data subject has, subject to subsection (3), given his or her consent to the processing._

_(3) Where the processing of personal data is to be carried out on the basis of the consent of the data subject referred to in subsection (2)(b), the processing shall be lawful only where, and to the extent that—_

_(a) having been informed of the intended purpose of the processing and the identity of the controller, the data subject gives his or her consent freely and explicitly,_

_(b) the request for consent is expressed in clear and plain language, and where such consent is given in the context of a written statement that also concerns other matters, the request for consent is presented to the data subject in a manner that is clearly distinguishable from those other matters, and_

_(c) the data subject may withdraw his or her consent at any time, and he or she shall be informed of this possibility prior to giving consent._

_(4) Where a data subject withdraws his or her consent to the processing of personal data pursuant to subsection (3)(c), the withdrawal of consent shall not affect the lawfulness of processing based on that consent prior to the consent being withdrawn._

_(5) Where a controller collects personal data for a purpose specified in section 70https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/2018/en/act/pub/0007/sec0070.html#sec70 (1)(a), the controller or another controller may process the data for a purpose so specified other than the purpose for which the data were collected, in so far as—_

_(a) the controller is authorised to process such personal data for such a purpose in accordance with the law of the European Union or the law of the State, and_

_(b) the processing is necessary and proportionate to the purpose for which the data are being processed._

*Option Grant and Exercise:*
Option grants and exercises for Russian (RUS) and Belarusian (BLR) citizens are compliant with applicable sanctions rules [(Council Regulation (EU) 2022/328)|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32022R0328&from=EN] if the respective RUS/BLR citizen holds a temporary or permanent EU residence permit at the time of the grant or exercise.
*Initial Public Offering (IPO):*
In the case of an IPO, RUS/BLR citizens must hold a temporary or permanent EU residence permit to be able to publicly trade Bolt shares. EU central securities depositories are prohibited from providing services related to securities issued after 12 April 2022 to RUS/BLR citizens unless they have an EU residence permit.
*Additional Considerations for Employee Liquidity Events (Pre-IPO):*
In addition to sanctions rules, there may be additional restrictions imposed by the relevant buyer on transactions involving RUS/BLR citizens during an employee liquidity event (pre-IPO). These restrictions are beyond Bolt's control and will depend on the policies and requirements of the relevant buyer, as has been the case with previous liquidity events.

Hi [~accountid:63fe21787c30bbd6b33e09d3] - you had asked me this:

_”_*_My question is:_* _Are there any issues with us determining the fees/fares/etc for the driver on their behalf from an agency perspective?Our current terms and conditions (clause 30.5 and 30.10) state that the taxi meter starts when the passenger enters the vehicle, however the driver is arguing against this. Legal is waiting to have a call with TFL (as it seems this driver is a serial complainer). I know that you are the master of the black cab agency model so wondered if you could give me a steer before I respond (if the driver has any valid arguments here).”_

I’ll set out some considerations for you here. 

Overall, in respect of strategy of dealing with this pre-claim correspondence, you may want to reach out to Burness Paul, who provided us with regulatory guidance on the black cabs model, after first syncing with the UK regulatory team for their view. 

*(1)* various resources on the launch of the feature and regulatory advice are available [here|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1AVPFBLB3Hfd2wmOUGWwnnNEdmaus8ilX].  Also see the launch channel here: [#uk-legal-2023-taxi-and-agency-launch|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C04SH7S8RBN]

This document is a little useful: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/12XBfbqY3eVR7u-8sJGIhf3Cd5f47CTyL/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/12XBfbqY3eVR7u-8sJGIhf3Cd5f47CTyL/edit|smart-link] 

*(2)* The rule of thumb with black cabs is that they may not charge more than the amounts prescribed by TfL from time to time, i.e. the on the meter rate. They may agree to charge less than this. Therefore the way that rates are set by our operations team (or at least as it should be) is that the fare is equivalent to or less than ‘on the meter’ rates. You will want to check this is still the case.

*(3)* The argument that is being entered into here is whether the time before the passenger gets into the cab is ‘regulatory time’ or not. Our obvious counter argument is that it is ‘obviously not’ and this is agreed to as a matter of fact of the arrangement. Drivers are at risk of passengers cancelling at get to charge a cancellation fee. Passengers are always at risk of drivers cancelling. That is the contractual position that is agreed to when offering services via the app. He is therefore ‘on journey’ from a regulatory perspective from the point in time that the passenger enters he cab. *Update:* 

* The *deadline to present our defense will not elapse until the end of September* – once the outside attorney has consulted the proceedings and verified the exact date of the writ of summons of the co-defendants they can give a more precise date.
* According to Portuguese law, when there is more than one defendant, as it is the case, the deadline of the last defendant to be summoned is applicable to the rest of the defendants. This means that if one of the defendants is domiciled abroad and benefits from a large term to present a defense – 60 days instead of the usual 30 days – the other defendants will also benefit from it. Since Bolt was summoned on 14 June, assuming that the other defendants were also summoned on the same date, the defendant base in Holland will benefit from 60 days, besides the court recess for summer between 16 July and 1^st^ September.

Thank you very much for the context, it is very helpful!

* If they agree to adjust the object of procurement to align with our model, all the best offers clauses as we amended them in the technical specification shall remain, because this is directly related to our services and business model. As a platform operator, we cannot assume full liability for the behavior, clothing, or vehicles of independent drivers, nor can we guarantee the quality of transportation services. By law, a platform operator is not allowed to control independent drivers or guarantee anything related to them. If we start controlling them, we risk having these independent drivers reclassified as our employees.

* However, to maintain the balance between the freedom of independent drivers and the quality of services offered via the Bolt platform, we have introduced various measures. For example, at the end of each journey, passengers are asked to provide feedback on the service provided. Bolt maintains a driver rating system accessible to passengers. If a driver fails to meet the minimum service requirements, we contact the driver, offer recommendations, and may require re-training. If there is no improvement, the driver is suspended from the platform. Additionally, we try to educate drivers by sending them comms, tips on how to improve performance. We have also introduced various safety features to provide more comfort to passengers, for example,
** *_Trip Anomaly -_* _a feature detects an anomaly and asks the drivers and riders if they need assistance. CS calls them / user is directed to 112_
** *_Rider Emergency Assist feature -_* _in-app Emergency Assist button to inform an emergency response team and a Safety team, who will make an immediate welfare call. Police not notified, button for calling 112 appears in the app._ 
** *_Phone masking_* - when a user makes a call via the Bolt app, his/her phone number remains hidden.
** *_Rider Trip Sharing_* - send the car's make, model, registration number, and live location to friends or family via a shareable link. All trips are also tracked and recorded.
** *_24/7 CS Safety team_*  
* Regarding the other clauses - OK, any adjustments will be added only to the special terms, with no changes to the general terms (BS). We can remove the reference to direct losses, provided the liability cap added as 13.12 to BS is included in the special terms. We can also retain clauses related to the acceptance act (even though, in practice, these clauses make no sense for our services).

I understand that there is a gap in procurement law when it comes to platform services, but some public companies in LT have managed to adjust the procurement object and accept our adjustments (Ignitis Group was flexible, and I believe the Bank of LT as well), so it is possible.

Good luck with the discussion, let me know afterwards how it went!

[~accountid:62d7b457807cf6f78ca9d117] - adjusting and expanding my guidance from Slack based on the new information I collected.

Overall - its a bit complicated:

* under the EU ePrivacy Directive, cross-pollination is ok, if it relates to similar products/offers form the same company. In this case, its likely similar enough, as we are reaching out to data subjects who are interested in work opportunities, not our products.
* however, is some jurisdictions, like in Poland, consumers can receive direct marketing only based on opt in consent - soft opt in rule is not recognised. This includes cross-pollination as well. Currently, we generally disregard this and rely on soft-opt in on the LCM level for all verticals for cross-pollination - its a business decision made by senior management.
* for Poland, based on the advice from our external counsels, opt-in consent is required both for B2B and B2C contexts - so it does not matter if the driver works with us via a legal person (LLC), as a sole proprietor, etc.

Also, please bear in mind that, as discussed in Slack, we expect a decision on direct marketing to be made in Poland in the upcoming weeks which will possibly affect our approach.

*To sum up, opt-in consent is required from drivers under Polish marketing laws in order to send them marketing for other products from Bolt. Any decision to depart from this approach would need to be approved by Marketing Leads as we would be at risk of receiving a fine for non-compliance*

Hello [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd] ,

We need to be compliant with the Romanian Legislation or we will be at risk of getting fined or even losing our license.

What are we doing at the moment is only applicable to drivers *blocked permanently due to fraudulent activities* and the process is as follows:

If a driver who has the account blocked only for fraudulent reasons contacts us, we will inform them that according to the local legislation and in accordance with our privacy policy, we are allowed to store their data for a certain period of time. Tier 1 is handling the deletion requests as it was updated in [*KB*|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/58951]. The only difference is that we do not untick the "GDPR" box located on their profiles and we do not place them on hidden. If we proceed with their account deletion requests they will take this as an opportunity to try and create a new "clean" account where they will resume their fraudulent activities.

For the ones who aren't blocked for fraudulent reasons we follow the already existing process from [*KB*|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/58951]. 

In this case, we believe that we are being compliant with the GDPR law as the European Commission mentions the following [*here*|https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/reform/rules-business-and-organisations/dealing-citizens/do-we-always-have-delete-personal-data-if-person-asks_en]:

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) gives individuals the right to ask for their data to be deleted and organisations do have an obligation to do so, except in the following cases: _there is a legal obligation to keep that data_; 

Thank you!
