hey Vilius.

{quote}This way, rider does not get charged for the trip at all and basically gets a free trip.{quote}

this is incorrect. we did try to charge the payment. if the payment goes through, all is well. but if we’re unable to collect the payment, then we refund the trip as Bolt shouldn’t be liable for an unapproved ride. in this case, the payment failed due to insufficient funds. 
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/2572951823|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/2572951823]

let me try to go over the logic of this process with you. the ride was initially requested with a predicted distance of 4.35km in a predicted duration of under 8min. then it ended up being 448.06km over 6 hours duration. when a rider places an order request in the Bolt App we run a fraud check, we decide whether to authorize or not the predicted amount from their account, and then only later if all is good we connect them with one of our drivers. that’s an approved ride. we ran our checks, and we connected the rider with the driver with the request to go from point A to point B. when a rider decides to change the destination of a ride, there’s another fraud check. we might allow or deny the change request. that’s due to fraud risk, where, for example, riders can initiate a request with a very short trip and then extend to a massive one, exactly like in this case. fraudsters use this strategy to cash out through driver accounts, as the driver still gets paid by Bolt but we don’t get any payment from the rider side. in this specific ride, [they tried 3 times to change the destination and we denied all 3 times|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/orderCalculationResults/ridehailing/order/edit/251/1663572896?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Atlantic%2FSt_Helena]. when we deny, both rider and driver get a message saying to drive to the original destination or to end the trip and make a new request. [this KB article|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7643088163474] should cover this topic (looks like article is broken and screenshots with the messages are not there. pls reach out to CSKM team about it). once we denied the changes and displayed the message, the driver *CHOSE* to ignore it and still fulfill the rider’s request. at this point, this trip isn’t approved by Bolt anymore, it’s just an agreement between two people inside a car. when that happens, we do our best not to punish the drivers, and that’s why we try to collect the money. we understand that there are similar trips in this scenario that are legit. but once we’re unable to capture the money, then the liability isn’t ours. 

I absolutely agree with you that this process isn’t neat and ideal for drivers as riders can use social engineering to deceive good drivers. if such rides are common, local teams can decide to deploy comms to drivers to educate them better on the topic or even improve onboarding processes to prevent this from happening. 

in terms of compensation, the deducted commission should obviously be paid back to the driver but we strongly advise to not compensate these offline unapproved trips back to drivers.

TLDR: after the investigation, no memory leak was found in the billing-artefact service.

As billing-artefact is working with the FS, it is expected that the WSS grows over the time (cause Linux might cache FS access). However, the memory is cleaned once it hits a certain limit (apparently it is 80%). Sometimes the alert falsely throws on fractional part difference, i.e. 0.80XXXX > 0.80, right before memory cleanup. I set up override, intended to stop such false-positive alerting, by increasing the warning limit by 0.01.

The fact that it was FS cache that caused WSS to grow is obvious when looking at the WSS - RSS graph: [https://nodemonitor.boltint.net/graph/d/kxFgnLQ7z/billing-service?orgId=1&var-project=billing-artefact&from=1721749784001&to=1721794249272&viewPanel=83|https://nodemonitor.boltint.net/graph/d/kxFgnLQ7z/billing-service?orgId=1&var-project=billing-artefact&from=1721749784001&to=1721794249272&viewPanel=83].

The RSS is stable (note that RSS doesn’t include FS cache in the aggregation).

!Screenshot 2024-07-26 at 01.59.39.png|width=406,height=301,alt="Screenshot 2024-07-26 at 01.59.39.png"!

*More detailed description of the project:*

*Problem*
Bolt Food app used to have only a single checkbox (“Allow sending news”) where users could either subscribe or unsubscribe from all marketing communications. It had the following negative implications:

* Lower marketing efficiency: users can’t unsubscribe from a subset of marketing communications. They can only unsubscribe from all of them at once.
* Lack of GDPR compliance: users are opted in to all marketing communications by default after signing up. Without granular consents we can’t change that behavior without significantly reducing our marketing efficiency. Lack of GDPR compliance puts Bolt at risk of fines up to 4% of GMV

*Solution*
We added a granular marketing consents management feature to the Bolt Food app. It is compliant with GDPR requirements and allows users to manage their marketing consents directly from the Bolt Food app.

Users can separately configure consents for each type of marketing communications (Bolt Products, Promotions and Tips, Partner Offers) and for each communication channel (email or push notifications).

Since we’ve implemented the NJSC rate limiter (almost) everywhere, we had to re-open the issue and restart the discussion, as it is included in the [Authentication Guidelines|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SEC/pages/4580409628/Authentication+guidelines+ASVS+V2] (future requirements) of Product Security. Your ground about lockout is correct, but some security is better than none. 

Even a 15-minute lockout will deter attackers without significantly inconveniencing customers(it doesn’t mean that we’re okay with 15 tho). It’s usually best to require users to reset their passwords after *X* number of failed attempts (lockout), and after the lockout, do not accept the correct password and never provide a hint if one of the future attempts does have correct password. 

Legitimate users can always contact Customer Service regarding locked-out accounts. This way, no one would be able to DoS us, especially since we do not leak existing user information (e.g., email addresses). We always recommend using Captcha simultaneously to double our security. I will be waiting for your response for this one.

“ Postovani gospodine Hausman, 

obračam Vam se povodom Vašeg upita Boltu od dana 18. lipnja 2024., a u kojem nas tražite pojašnjenje što se podrazumijeva pod nepropisno ostavljanje i šta podliježe uklanjanju unutar 120min.

U skladu s Vašim upitom, u nastavku Vam dostavljamo traženo. 



Pregledom ugovora izmeďu Bolta i Grada OSijeka, nismo pronašli odredbu koja se točno referira na ovu problematiku uklanjanja nepropisno ostavljenih romobila unutar 120 minuta. Ako smo u krivu, ljubazno Vas molimo da nam ukažete na članak kojim je navedeno propisano. 

Takoďer, u samom javnom pozivu, ali i Prilogu 3., koji je sastavni dio javnog poziva, navodi se ova obvezna karakteristika sustava: Uklanjanje nepropisno ostavljenih i parkiranih E-romobila. 

Na temelju toga, u opisu naše ponude, detaljnije smo opisali na koji način vršimo uklanjanje nepropisno ostavljenih ili parkiranih romobila. 

Prvenstveno željeli bi istaknuti koje su situacije koje, prema našem nahođenju, podrazumijevaju nepropisno ostavljene ili parkirane romobile:



* Romobil koji je neovlaštenim korištenjem ostavljen izvan zone korištenja E-romobila kako je definirana javnim pozivom.
* Romobil koji je iz nekog razloga ostavljen unutar zone zabrane parkiranja kako je definirano javnim pozivom (prazna baterija, neovlašteno rukovanje romobilom itd.)
* Romobil koji je neovlaštenim rukovanjem ostavljen unutar zone zabrane vožnje kako je definirano javnim pozivom.
* Romobil koji je iz nekog razloga ostavljen na nečijem privatnom posjedu (prazna baterija, nepropisno rukovanje itd.)

* Takoďer, i situacije koje su definirane Clankom 84. Zakona o sigurnosti prometa na cestama. 

U našoj ponudi smo naveli 5 kanala putem kojih korisnici ili građani mogu prijaviti problem s romobilom koji uzrokuje prepreku, opasnost ili se nesmotreno koristi. 

Prvenstveno, Bolt se ponajviše oslanja na dojave korisnika, drugih građana ili javnih službi.

Drugi način detekcije problema je putem telematskih podataka romobila preko akcelerometra koji mogu otkriti je li se romobil prevrnuo, pomiče li se silom ili je oštećen. Ovaj način detekcije nije moguć ako je matična ploča romobila prethodno razbijena ili oštećena jer ga sustav tada više ne prepoznaje.

Naš tim za žurnu reakciju u slučajevima nepropisnog ostavljanja/parkiranja ima prosječno vrijeme reakcije od 120 minuta. Dakle, u najboljoj mogućoj mjeri se trudimo da u svakoj situaciji reagiramo unutar 120 minuta.

U slucaju potrebe za bilo kakvim daljnjim pojašnjenjima ili dodatnim pitanjima, slobodno nam se obratite.

Srdačan pozdrav, “

A Commission de Sécurité is a safety commission in France that ensures public buildings meet specific safety standards. This commission is responsible for conducting inspections and approving the safety measures of buildings, particularly in areas like fire safety, emergency exits, and overall compliance with safety regulations.

We will need assistance with the procedures to create the necessary files for urban planning. Currently, we are not fully compliant, so our first step is to request a Notice de Sécurité (Safety Notice) and initiate a Mission SEI.

A Notice de Sécurité is a document that outlines the safety features and measures of a building, ensuring they comply with the required safety standards. It includes details such as fire safety systems, evacuation plans, and structural safety features.

A Mission SEI is a mission focused on the safety of industrial establishments. This involves a comprehensive review and assessment of the safety protocols, infrastructure, and emergency preparedness of industrial facilities. The goal is to identify potential risks and ensure that all safety measures are in place and effective.

We need support in navigating these processes and compiling the necessary documentation to ensure compliance with all safety and urban planning regulations.

*Context:*

* Scammers are trying to impersonate Bolt CS via in-app chat and phishing for account details. This allows them to overtake access to the account, withdrawing driver funds, or ordering with a rider account.
* We detect user credentials (phone number and email address) from both rider and driver and suppress those when shared in the in-app chat, even after translation; that means any personal information requested is hidden from the chat

* *How phishing is done for riders:*

* while waiting to be picked up, riders are asked for their phone number and 4-digit code to confirm the ride. From what passengers shared so far, it seems that the codes are then used to bypass the 2-factor verification of their email address or Bolt/Uber app.

* *How phishing is done for drivers:*

* some drivers reported that they received a message from a passenger saying “you are about to pick up a VIP passenger, please confirm your phone number and the 4-digit code”. Compromised driver accounts are found either through reports from passengers or they claim they have no idea how the details got changed, so it’s hard to track how exactly the phishing happened.

*Reactive measures that we apply:*

* Currently, we don’t ask drivers to come to the hub but we use the Onfido selfie verification to verify their identity. We block them as soon as any report comes in, HP team calls them to verify the correct details and devices over the phone, and blocks any new devices. Once all done, we unblock the account with a scheduled selfie verification.

The plan was to launch Bolt Boost on August 1, 2024, with an internal deadline to publish the terms and conditions by July 1, 2024.

Initially, the business used Deloitte’s recommended method to calculate the National Living Wage (NLW) as follows:

(Driver’s earnings + incentives) - (vehicle expenses + CCZ fee + tools)

If the result is below the minimum NLW amount, the driver receives a top-up to reach the minimum NLW.

[^Deloitte Advice 1- Review of NMW, HP and AE proposal.pdf]

* Before publishing T&Cs, Tarun gave strong reccomendations not to deduct  CCZ fee in the amount of 15 pounds.  He advised the same as we are using the flat fee for costs is based on HMRC guidelines to deduct only £1.50 per ride contribution towards the Congestion Charge Zone (CCZ) fees to account for multi-app usage. Deducting the full £15 CCZ fee would incentivize drivers to work minimally with us and more with competitors, leading to unintended financial advantages for them. Consistency in handling CCZ fees and other expenses, such as holiday pay deductions, is crucial for a fair and rational policy.

[https://drive.google.com/file/d/10jfjhRciuIMaEDJrIFZ29zuq6seE4a9f/view?usp=sharing|https://drive.google.com/file/d/10jfjhRciuIMaEDJrIFZ29zuq6seE4a9f/view?usp=sharing|smart-link] 

* 15th or July - Based on this Gareth and the business have decided to proceed with the launch without deducting £15 per day but only £1.50 per ride. 

[Recommendations from the business |https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vi7oBL_GggxcmyhaI40Cp5n-Hj5W4wpB-2-nxxHQSPQ/edit?usp=sharing]

* We obtained opinion from Deloitte on the changed methodology - [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1RLgFo-X3XjEPK5UEOAkYAfCx5KIGBbs4/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1RLgFo-X3XjEPK5UEOAkYAfCx5KIGBbs4/edit|smart-link] 
* Business discussions on July 12th, 2024. - [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C04PSRGJ8RE/p1720782964451449?thread_ts=1720770629.447829&cid=C04PSRGJ8RE|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C04PSRGJ8RE/p1720782964451449?thread_ts=1720770629.447829&cid=C04PSRGJ8RE|smart-link] Gareth taylor: “My recommendation would be as follows:
*# We don’t put any details of the calculation for the National Living Wage Top-up in any of our communications going out this month.
*# This buys us some more time to make a final decision on this.
*# In the interim, we go with what I’ve proposed as the calculation. If we realise that we need to change the calculation to the £15 calculation, then we do so.
*# This would result in the drivers getting more of a pay-out.
*# The rationale for this is that it’s easier to pay the drivers more than to pay them less.
*# Then when we have sufficient clarity on the formula, we can give more explicit comms to the drivers about exactly how it’s calculated.
* The above does not take into consideration the approach to the Settlement Strategy and any disclosures needed there.[@christian.berces|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U01B4UDNC59] is the decision maker. However, I’m not sure (i) how much additional information he needs on this; and (ii) which individuals from the Management Team he would want to approve of this decision.”

Christian Berces:

“Option 1 and 2 in the [document|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vi7oBL_GggxcmyhaI40Cp5n-Hj5W4wpB-2-nxxHQSPQ/edit] make sense to me, unless I’m missing something big. Perhaps the two points we should work on:

* We should cap the CCZ revenues and expenses to 15£; if not for launch, then with a reasonable ETA

Hey [~accountid:6071993aef87dd006894d4bd], thank you for the request!

As mentioned in the [🌍 Issue type adding guidelines|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/6336739310226], an issue tag for an outgoing case should be added *only* if the user we reached out to raises a new issue in the case. Otherwise, outgoing cases should be left _untagged_, and this pertains to both safety and non-safety cases.

The current [🚨 Safety escalation guidelines|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/11165229227154] are being revamped and soon will be updated _(a tentative timeline is the beginning of August)_, but the general idea for case tagging for the situation you described is already included there:

{quote}* If equipped to deal with the issue yourself, handle the non-safety part once the safety investigation is concluded
* If not equipped to deal with such an issue, de-escalate the case to Tier 1 (keeping *both* the Severity level and the Safety issue tag/s) once you conclude the safety investigation
* *Safety agents* are responsible for adding/removing only Safety issue tags when escalating/de-escalating a case. A non-safety agent will add non-safety issue tags.
* *Non-safety agents* are responsible for adding/removing only non-safety issue tags when escalating/de-escalating a case. A Safety agent will add the relevant Safety issue tags.{quote}

What’s currently missing from the guidelines is that if the safety agent is equipped to deal with the newly raised non-safety issue within the outgoing case, they should also add the relevant non-safety issue tags since no escalation is taking place and we do have cross-skilled agents who work both on Tier 1 and Safety. However, this will be updated with the release of the new escalation guidelines and safety workflow.

Additionally, I also have a task in my backlog to work on the [🐝 Creating outgoing cases|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/4405977630738] article and other case-tagging-related articles as, at the moment, information on overall case tagging is widely scattered, and it can be difficult for agents to find coherent guidelines. 

With all this in mind, please bear with us for just a little bit longer. We’re working tirelessly to ensure the KB is up-to-date with the relevant information and guidelines for agents, and very soon, all of the mentioned articles will be updated. 

I will be closing this ticket, but if there are any other comments, concerns or questions on the topic, or if there’s anything else we can help you with, feel free to reach out.

Thank you, and have a nice day! 🙂

Some additional analysis on possible practical solution:

For us main problem so far was unexpected alerts (payment instrument type and id not matching) and spent resources on investigation. Problem itself coming from human error in some price scraping botnet or custom fleet tool in Berlin (assumption from thread with fraud team). However some EU cities have similar requests, but less than 100 requests per day.

I don’t think it would be proper to suppress all such errors (payment instrument type and id not matching) because we will have a chance to not react on real misconfiguration in mobile app, for example. However, we can try to localise the problem recognising the pattern (return empty/junk response for requests - Berlin, processout/cash instrument, and see if botnet/tool reacts).

If we won’t skip all such errors, we probably won’t will be able to fix all the noise. We can reduce it if:

# most active users (top of the list for the problem are doing around 1000 ride search requests per day) are marked as bots (manually by fraud team or by bot detection scripts)
## bot detection currently is not detecting all of such users ([thread message|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/CNV6QMK89/p1720190300967179?thread_ts=1720173896.372869&cid=CNV6QMK89]) so it’ll be up to product teams to improve queries
# in commerce-gateway we start recognising bot users (calling user api for each user or receiving isBot from mobile app, if possible) and returning some junk response for bot users.

Some users involved seem to have very low request count, so they won’t be marked as bots, thus some noise will stay anyway.

{quote}After many discussions with the agent (landlord does not speak english) - the only clause which they accepted from our side is the one which allows us to pull back from the contract unless enough electrical power is provided.

In the light of aforementioned I need to provide my advice regarding potential consequences of going through with the deal on the conditions that are currently proposed by the Landlord (LL). Legal team cannot prevent you from accepting the deal, but you need to understand that any negative consequences resulting from poorly negotiated terms of the agreement will be borne by you. Here is the list of the main concerns regarding the proposed agreement:

* Article 2 - we always need to specify the use of the property because we will store dangerous objects and we need LL to confirm that they are ok with this. Without stating the purpose of the use of the warehouse we risk LL saying that they were unaware and in case of an accident blame us for improper use of the property. Accidents with warehouse are quite common for Bolt and therefore we need to be extra cautious with this.
* Article 3 (2) and (3) - LL insists on automatic renewal of the lease and we normally try to avoid it, because it is hard for us to track some deadlines and we don't want the lease to be renewed in case we miss the deadline to notify about the termination.
* Article 4 (3) - the deposit should not be used to cover all expenses, but it should be used only to cover direct losses and costs. Therefore, there is a risk that this money will be used for things that should not be covered by deposit and we will not be able to rely on it.
* Article 6 (1) - for us it is important to get confirmation that warehouse will be in a condition suitable for our intended use (which should be specified in Article 2) and that they can provide enough electricity power. Without these confirmations we cannot be sure that the place will meet our standards and we will not be able to impose these standards after the contract will be signed.
* Article 13 - without cap on the rent price increase we cannot predict rent price changes.
* Article 14 - we proposed to list LL's obligations and crucial ones are obligation to maintain the property in a condition suitable for our purpose and fitting necessary fire prevention equipment. As mentioned earlier, e-scooters and batteries are dangerous objects that are prone to starting fire. Without these provisions Bolt will not be able to shift liability on the LL in case of a fire at the warehouse.
* Article 17 (4) - obligation to provide electricity is on us and we are also obliged to ensure that our use does not disturb the infrastructure. This is particularly worrying as we may require more electricity that can be considered "normal" and obligations to sort things out are on us.
* Article 17 (8) - it is prohibited to keep materials that have increased risk of fire unless these are included in the scope of our activity. There is no specification in the agreement what is included in the scope of our activity and this point may be disputed.
* Article 25 - our liability is unlimited.
* Article 27 - we can be evicted easily and after one occasion of non-payment of the rent.

Please note that there is still some information missing from the agreement that needs to be filled in:

* Information about contracting parties at the start of the agreement;
* Article 3 (1);
* Article 34 (1).

First of all, 3 days seems not long enough for us, as an organisation, to process such topic so I suggest 7 days (or at least 5) for us to notify the customer. Second of all, this period should be counted from the day Bolt became aware of the damage, not from the day it occurred. Imagine that a damage occurred on 1 July 2024 but we became aware of it on 10 July 2024. In such wording of the customer, we would not be entitled to claim any damage.

Customer agrees to indemnify any cost or damage to Bolt or any other person arising from User’s use of the Bolt Services or User’s violation of applicable Romanian law, provided that the Customer is notified of such damage caused by the User as soon as possible, but no later than {color:#ff5630}-3- {color}{color:#36b37e}7{color} days from the date {color:#ff5630}-the damage occurred-{color} {color:#36b37e}of when Bolt became aware of the damage{color}. [~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] I suggest we have a quick sync on this before I respond, but my thoughts on Nils-Eric’s response are as follows:

* There appears to be a clear _business case_ for simplifying the process and not asking for driver consent (i.e., the FO are having to eat the cost for the period during which drivers cannot yet access the Bolt app, and the process would be a lot quicker if handled by CS). However, *this does not in any way change the legal position* - to change a driver’s personal data, we need the request to either come from the driver or from someone properly authorised.
* Nils-Eric refers to German labor law and the “_clear framework of employment_” that justifies this process change. I do not fully understand the point that he is trying to make here, but I highly doubt it changes our GDPR analysis on the issues.
* We _could_ consider changing the process such that we ask the Fleet Owner to provide us with a +general authorisation+ from the driver to change their username / phone number / email address where so required. The GDPR does not explicitly prevent this, and this would mean that we would only need to ask for a driver’s authorisation once (and could thereafter change the driver’s account details without specifically seeking the driver’s consent to do so). However if we chose this option, we would need to (1) agree on what wording we could accept in any general authorisations (as these would need to be clear, specific and verifiable from our side); (2) examine our verification processes to make sure that we are still being compliant; and (3) ensure that there is a system in place for drivers who want to withdraw such authorisation. On balance, *I am not sure that this is worth the effort*, given that this seems more like a “it would be nice to have this” rather than “we need this”, and there are still some compliance risks with the general authorisation approach, but let me know if you disagree.
* Overall, I think the best approach here would be to respond firmly and clearly, saying the following - {color:#4c9aff}*do you agree?*{color}
** The current process should still be kept as it is, as the legal position has not changed. We need rectification requests to either come from the driver or someone who is properly authorised - otherwise, we will be non-compliant with the GDPR and risk possible data breaches. Although we appreciate that there is a business case here, we still need to respect the legal position on this.

After looking more closely into replacing the Strapi locale picker with a custom component, I’ve noticed a couple of concerning points.

Our goal is to inject a custom component instead of this one: [LocalePicker.tsx|https://github.com/strapi/strapi/blob/v5/main/packages/plugins/i18n/admin/src/components/LocalePicker.tsx]. However, this component relies on some internal helpers/hooks that are not exposed, such as {{useI18n}} and {{useGetLocalesQuery}}.

While we could copy these over, they include not only localization-specific logic but also some permissions-related logic, which introduces the risk of them becoming outdated as Strapi updates.Another approach is to create a forked version of i18n.

However, given its complexity and the likelihood of future updates, this might be risky at this stage. Given these challenges, I suggest we put the selector improvement on hold for now. We can revisit this when Strapi improves the internal plugin exports or if we find a better solution.

* Credit: Everything that should NOT be in the payout.

Hey,

*Long answer:* Article 17 of the GDPR provides for the “right to be forgotten”.  It states, “The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay and the controller shall have the obligation to erase personal data without undue delay” if one of a number of conditions applies. “Undue delay” is considered to be about a month. You must also take reasonable steps to verify the person requesting erasure is actually the data subject.

This therefore means that a driver may request for their information to be deleted from our systems. We process this request on the PARTNER ACCOUNT level by changing the status to “DELETED”.

*Short answer*: If there was a request to “delete” the account, please proceed in accordance with the process and change the status to “DELETED”

To be clear - *we should still be sending them the DSA*.

The vendor is technically correct that a DSA is not _mandatory_ (under the GDPR) where both parties are acting as independent controllers (as appears to be the case here). However, we still push for a DSA whenever we are sharing personal data with third parties (again, as appears to be the case here) - this helps ensure certainty regarding the roles of the parties, and that Bolt is properly protected should the vendor in any way compromise the personal data of the drivers. We are also entering into a DSA with all other vendors assisting with Bolt Rewards, so we should also do so here.

As such, I would be grateful if you could revert to the vendor and flag the following:

* We appreciate that a DSA is not legally mandatory where both parties are acting as independent controllers. However, it is Bolt’s standard practice to enter into a DSA whenever relevant personal data are shared with third parties. This helps to ensure, among other things, contractual certainty and data security.
* The DSA provided is based on Bolt’s standard DSA. The vendor should review it, populate it with any missing information and confirm whether they are happy with it. If the vendor has any comments / suggested edits to the DSA, they should clearly explain why the edits are necessary.
